pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria THE SMOKING GUN: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam paired with profound hyponatremia and urine that turns a port-wine color upon exposure to light, triggered by fasting and a sulfonamide drug. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant metabolic disorder caused by a partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), a key enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Triggers such as low-carbohydrate fasting, emotional stress, or CYP450-inducing medications (like sulfonamide antibiotics) upregulate hepatic delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1). This causes a massive accumulation of neurotoxic heme precursors, specifically delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These toxic intermediates induce autonomic neurotoxicity (manifesting as severe hypertension and tachycardia), visceral neuropathic pain without localized peritoneal signs, central nervous system toxicity (acute psychosis, SIADH leading to hyponatremia), and peripheral motor neuropathy. When exposed to air and ambient light, excess urinary PBG oxidizes into porphobilin, imparting the classic dark red or port-wine coloration to the urine.
